item.title: Your Optimizer Is (Approximately) Doing Fisher Flow
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Adam, K-FAC, and EWC are all propagating Fisher information with different approximation structures. Here's the math, the code, and the caveats.
item.content:encoded:
Most people who use Adam don’t think about Fisher information. But Adam’s second moment estimate is doing something specific: it’s tracking a diagonal approximation to the empirical Fisher Information Matrix and using it to precondition the gradient. K-FAC does the same thing with a Kronecker-factored approximation. EWC uses the Fisher as a regularization penalty. Natural gradient uses the full Fisher.

These connections are not new. Amari formalized natural gradient in 1998. Khan and Rue unified many of these algorithms under a single Bayesian learning rule in 2023. Martens wrote the definitive 76-page survey of natural gradient methods in 2020. Kunstner, Hennig, and Balles showed important limitations of the empirical Fisher approximation in 2019.

What I built is a small pedagogical package (fisherflow) that lets you verify these connections with working code. This post walks through what I learned while building it.

Fisher Information in 30 Seconds

You have a parametric model $p(x | \theta)$. The score function is the gradient of the log-likelihood: $s(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \log p(x|\theta)$. The Fisher Information Matrix is the expected outer product of the score:

$$\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[s(\theta) s(\theta)^\top\right]$$

This is also $-\mathbb{E}[\nabla^2_\theta \log p(x|\theta)]$, the expected negative Hessian. It measures how much information the data carries about the parameters. High Fisher information means the likelihood is sharply peaked, so the data tells you a lot.

The key property: Fisher information from independent observations adds up.

$$\mathcal{I}_{1:n}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathcal{I}_{x_i}(\theta)$$

This additivity is what makes sequential estimation clean. You maintain a running estimate $\hat\theta_t$ and accumulated information $\mathcal{I}_t$, and when new data arrives you just add the new information and take a natural gradient step:

$$\mathcal{I}_t = \mathcal{I}_{t-1} + \mathcal{I}_{\text{new}}$$

$$\hat\theta_t = \hat\theta_{t-1} + \mathcal{I}_t^{-1} \cdot s_t$$

The $\mathcal{I}_t^{-1}$ preconditioner is what makes this a natural gradient rather than a vanilla gradient. It rescales the step to account for the curvature of the statistical manifold.

The Optimizer Taxonomy

Different optimizers approximate the Fisher at different levels. The approximation determines the computational cost and the quality of the preconditioning:

Method Fisher approximation Cost What’s lost
SGD $\mathcal{I} = \lambda I$ (scalar) $O(1)$ All curvature information
Adam $\mathcal{I} = \text{diag}(v)$ (diagonal) $O(d)$ Off-diagonal interactions
K-FAC $\mathcal{I} \approx A \otimes B$ (Kronecker) $O(m^3 + n^3)$ Cross-layer interactions
Natural gradient Full $\mathcal{I}$ $O(d^3)$ Nothing (but intractable for large $d$)

The package lets you verify this. Here’s the Adam case.

Adam Is Simplified Diagonal Fisher Flow

Adam’s second moment $\hat{v}t = \beta_2 \hat{v}{t-1} + (1-\beta_2) g_t^2$ is tracking the diagonal of an exponentially-weighted empirical Fisher. But the equivalence isn’t exact. It holds under specific simplifications:

  1. No bias correction (remove the $1/(1 - \beta_2^t)$ term)
  2. No epsilon
  3. Use $v_t$ directly instead of $\sqrt{v_t}$ (this one matters: Adam uses a square-root preconditioner, not the standard natural gradient preconditioner)
  4. The “Fisher” Adam estimates is the empirical Fisher (outer product of gradients at current parameters), not the true Fisher (expectation under the model’s own distribution). These differ away from convergence (Kunstner et al., 2019).

The fisherflow package has an AdamAsFisherFlow class that maintains two parallel parameter trajectories: one via simplified Adam, one via diagonal Fisher Flow with exponential forgetting. They match to machine precision:

from fisherflow import AdamAsFisherFlow
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)
conn = AdamAsFisherFlow(d=5, lr=0.01, beta2=0.999)

for step in range(50):
    grad = np.random.randn(5)
    conn.verify_equivalence(grad)  # asserts match to 1e-12

print("All 50 steps matched.")

The full Adam (with sqrt, bias correction, epsilon) diverges from the Fisher Flow version. You can see exactly where and by how much:

conn_full = AdamAsFisherFlow(d=3, lr=0.01, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8)
conn_ff = AdamAsFisherFlow(d=3, lr=0.01, beta2=0.999)

grad = np.random.randn(3)
theta_adam = conn_full.step_adam_full(grad)
theta_ff = conn_ff.step_fisher_flow(grad)

print(f"Gap: {np.linalg.norm(theta_adam - theta_ff):.6f}")
# Non-zero — the simplifications matter.

This is pedagogically useful because it makes the connection concrete while being honest about the caveats. He (2024) provides a more rigorous treatment in the FAdam paper.

EWC Is Trivially Fisher Regularization

Elastic Weight Consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) uses the Fisher Information Matrix directly in its loss function. There is no approximation to demonstrate here, because EWC was defined this way:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{EWC}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{new}}(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \sum_i F_i (\theta_i - \theta_i^*)^2$$

where $F_i$ is the diagonal Fisher from the previous task and $\theta^*$ is the old parameter vector. The Fisher serves as an importance weight: parameters with high Fisher information were important for the old task and should be changed less.

The fisherflow package verifies this identity is exact:

from fisherflow import EWCAsFisherFlow

conn = EWCAsFisherFlow(d=4, lambda_ewc=1.0)

# Train on task 1
for _ in range(20):
    conn.step_task(np.random.randn(4))
conn.consolidate()

# EWC penalty === Fisher regularization (by construction)
theta_new = conn.theta + 0.1 * np.random.randn(4)
assert conn.ewc_penalty(theta_new) == conn.fisher_regularization(theta_new)

When the Theory Applies (and When It Doesn’t)

There are two regimes for Fisher information in optimization:

Classical regime. You train to convergence. The Fisher at the optimum is the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood. Asymptotic theory applies: the MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal, and achieves the Cramer-Rao bound. Fisher-based uncertainty quantification is meaningful.

Modern ML regime. You stop before convergence (because of computational budgets, or because early stopping helps generalization). The Fisher information accumulated along the trajectory is not the Fisher at the optimum. It encodes something about the path you took through parameter space, not about the curvature at a stationary point.

This distinction matters because most of the elegant theory (information additivity, Cramer-Rao efficiency, uncertainty quantification via $\mathcal{I}^{-1}$) assumes you’re in the classical regime. In the modern regime, the accumulated Fisher acts more like an implicit regularizer than a curvature estimate.

Barrett and Dherin (2021) showed that SGD with finite learning rate implicitly penalizes the trace of the empirical Fisher. Jastrzebski et al. (2021) showed that the Fisher trace early in training critically affects generalization. The takeaway: Fisher information dynamics during training matter, but they mean something different from what the classical theory describes.

What I Got Wrong (and What the Review Taught Me)

I originally wrote a 56-page paper claiming this unification as a contribution. A thorough review revealed that the unification was already achieved more completely by Khan and Rue (2023) from a Bayesian perspective, and that Martens (2020) had covered most of the same theoretical ground. Several of my proofs were wrong (I conflated natural gradient flow with geodesic flow, claimed a conservation law for a dissipative system, and “proved” emergence from a circular definition). The experiments were invalid because all random seeds produced identical results.

So I pivoted to building the pedagogical package instead. The value is not in the unification itself (that’s been done) but in having executable code that lets you verify the connections and see exactly where the approximations break down.

The package is at github.com/queelius/fisher-flow. It includes 5 tutorial notebooks that walk through everything in this post with live code.

References

  • Amari, S. (1998). Natural gradient works efficiently in learning. Neural Computation, 10(2), 251-276.
  • Khan, M.E. and Rue, H. (2023). The Bayesian Learning Rule. JMLR, 24(281), 1-76.
  • Martens, J. (2020). New Insights and Perspectives on the Natural Gradient Method. JMLR, 21(146), 1-76.
  • Kunstner, F., Hennig, P., and Balles, L. (2019). Limitations of the Empirical Fisher Approximation. NeurIPS.
  • Kirkpatrick, J. et al. (2017). Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks. PNAS, 114(13), 3521-3526.
  • Martens, J. and Grosse, R. (2015). Optimizing Neural Networks with Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature. ICML.
  • He, D. (2024). FAdam: Adam is a natural gradient optimizer using diagonal empirical Fisher information. ICLR 2025.
  • Barrett, D.G.T. and Dherin, B. (2021). Implicit Gradient Regularization. ICLR.
  • Jastrzebski, S. et al. (2021). Catastrophic Fisher Explosion. ICML.
  • Davis, O. et al. (2024). Fisher Flow Matching for Generative Modeling over Discrete Data. NeurIPS. (Note: different “Fisher Flow,” same manifold.)

item.title: Fisher Flow: Optimization on the Statistical Manifold
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Gradient descent in Euclidean space ignores the geometry of probability distributions. Natural gradient descent uses the Fisher information metric instead. Fisher Flow makes this continuous.
item.content:encoded:
Standard gradient descent treats parameter space as flat. It uses Euclidean distance, which means the same step size in parameter space can produce wildly different changes in the distribution depending on where you are. Fisher Flow fixes this by optimizing along the natural geometry of probability distributions.

The Geometry of Distributions

Probability distributions form a Riemannian manifold. The Fisher information matrix provides the natural metric on this manifold:

FIM: I(theta) = E[grad log p(x|theta) grad log p(x|theta)^T]

This captures how sensitive the distribution is to parameter changes. It is the curvature of the likelihood surface. It tells you the true gradient direction in parameter space, not the Euclidean one.

Natural Gradient vs. Standard Gradient

Standard gradient descent updates parameters in Euclidean space:

theta_{t+1} = theta_t - alpha grad L(theta_t)

This is inefficient because it ignores parameter correlations. A step of size epsilon in one direction might barely change the distribution while the same step in another direction changes it drastically.

Natural gradient descent uses the Fisher metric:

theta_{t+1} = theta_t - alpha I(theta_t)^{-1} grad L(theta_t)

Pre-multiplying by the inverse Fisher information rescales the gradient to account for the local geometry. The key property: natural gradient is invariant to reparametrization. It does not matter how you choose to represent your distributions.

Fisher Flow

Fisher Flow makes this continuous:

dtheta/dt = -I(theta)^{-1} grad L(theta)

This defines a flow on the parameter manifold. Loss decreases monotonically along the flow. The trajectories follow the natural geometry. Step size adapts automatically because the curvature scales the updates.

The Practical Problem

Computing I(theta)^{-1} is expensive. For a neural network with n parameters, the full Fisher information matrix is n x n, and inverting it is O(n^3). That is not practical for modern networks.

Approximations help. Diagonal Fisher approximation is cheap but crude. Block-diagonal Fisher captures within-layer correlations. K-FAC (Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature) approximates the Fisher with Kronecker products, bringing computation down to O(n). That makes it practical for real networks.

def fisher_flow_step(params, loss_fn, data):
    # Compute gradient
    grad = compute_gradient(loss_fn, params, data)

    # Estimate Fisher information (diagonal approx)
    fisher = estimate_fisher_diagonal(params, data)

    # Natural gradient step
    natural_grad = grad / (fisher + epsilon)

    # Update parameters
    params = params - learning_rate * natural_grad

    return params

Variational Inference

Fisher flow gives a natural framework for variational inference. You have a variational distribution q(z|phi) and you want to minimize KL[q(z|phi) || p(z|x)]. Following the Fisher geometry of q means your optimization respects the structure of the distribution family you are searching over.

What the Theory Says

Fisher flow converges to local optima. The convergence rate depends on the conditioning of the Fisher information matrix. The flow is stable under perturbations, and the natural gradient provides implicit regularization.

The important theoretical property is geometric: the optimization respects the underlying probability manifold structure and is invariant to reparametrization. If you switch from mean/variance to natural parameters, the flow does not change. That is a strong property.

Open Questions

Higher-order geometry (third-order information) could improve convergence near saddle points. Dynamic FIM approximation quality, adjusting the fidelity of your Fisher approximation as training progresses, is worth exploring. And extending Fisher flow to infinite-dimensional (non-parametric) settings is an open theoretical problem.
